author: Joni Hilton
title: You Have Survived 100% of Your Bad Days - Meridian Magazine
text:
A couple recently moved into our ward. They had met at a homeless shelter. She was a member, and he joined after meeting her. Their wedding was beautiful; he cried openly with tears of joy. They’re both excited to have a home of their own, now.
A few weeks ago, she mentioned in Relief Society, that the shelter had a sign on the wall, which said, “You Have Survived 100% of Your Bad Days.” We all chuckled, but we also realized there was great truth there.
Too often we catastrophize. Some people do it more than others, but we are all tempted to assume the worst, lose all hope, and play mental images of all the disasters we can imagine. We turn up the worry knob and give into panic.
The bride’s mother could think , Oh, no—the florist is late to the wedding reception—what if they don’t even show up?
A pregnant women could think , the baby isn’t moving enough. Oh my gosh–maybe it has a terrible condition of some kind…
A student might think , I’m going to fail. It’s my worst subject and I’ll bet I’m already way behind everyone else.
These are all examples of borrowing trouble, and assuming the very worst will happen. We write a whole, distorted narrative about how badly our job interview will go, how confusing our new calling will be, how we won’t impress our date’s parents.
This negative self-talk can immobilize us if we don’t get control of it. Doctors say it can lead to unnecessary anxiety, depression, OCD, and a miserable life! It may have begun in childhood, as the brain’s way to protect us from bad news. But we need to get past it, see life in a more realistic light, and stop always assuming the worst.
It also blocks us from exercising faith. It can make us reluctant to pray because we’re sure everything will go sideways anyhow. It can make us feel forgotten by God, something none of us ever are.
And it robs us of joyful anticipation of the future. How much healthier would we be if we assumed the best of things and good outcomes, instead of catastrophe?
Psychologists say we can regain control by making deliberate, consistent efforts to replace these exaggerated thoughts with more realistic ones. You could even say to yourself, “Okay, there’s a wild one again, I’m not buying into that…” Talking out loud can actually interrupt the fatalistic spiral. If something triggers you, practice deep-breathing exercises, and meditation, as well.
Involve the Lord. Ask for the Holy Ghost to stay close by, and guide you away from scary thoughts. Keep a list of your talents and strengths. Remind yourself that you are not a magnet for trouble, but a child of God who is growing and learning all the time.
Know in your heart that you’re a good person. Yes, trials come into all our lives. But yours do not have to be identified before they even happen! Be aware and recognize worries, then deliberately imagine the opposite: Great success. Peace. A joyful outcome. When you catch yourself thinking in extremes, identify it and pull back from the cliff. Imagine happier results. Success. Contentment.
Experts also advise taking good care of your health, and getting enough sleep. They also recommend taking a social media break. To much online is intentionally extreme, going for shock value. Even ads seem bent on catastrophizing the situation their product can allegedly “treat.”
Our thoughts are not always facts, are they? In fact, when we dig a little deeper, there might be no evidence at all to support a quick assumption.
Think how the adversary uses this tendency—we feel prompted to share the gospel with someone, but then Satan pops up and tells us that person would never be interested, and might even have some harsh words for you. We decide to do better at Temple attendance, then the devil reminds us that we didn’t understand everything perfectly, and we should stay home. This same formula could work with keeping the word of wisdom, paying tithing, ministering to our assigned members, fulfilling callings—he’s the master of lies and overstatements. Catastrophizing is exactly what he’d love all of us to do!
Will we still have bad days ? Of course. No one’s life sings along forever on pink flower petals and joyful news. But we can, as the shelter sign says, survive every one of them, and still find joy and contentment through closeness with the Holy Ghost. The key is this: Whom do we listen to?
Joni Hilton is the author of dozens of best-selling LDS books. She was a script writer for Music and the Spoken Word for 30 years, and shares hundreds of life hacks as the Youtube Mom. Find them on her website at http://www.jonihilton.com/
